title: Commentarii In Porphyrium A Se Translatum
author: Boethius

passages.original: quam uim, nisi prius de generibus, speciebus, propriis et differentiis noti- tiam scientiamque perceperis, nullo umquam tempore discer- nes. Idem Aristoteles ait quid sint primae substantiae. quid secundae. et primas substantias dicit esse indiuiduorum corporum et singulorum, ut est Cicero aut Plato aut Socrates, secundas uero substantias species appellauit, ut est homo, uel genera, in quibus ipsae species continentur, ut est animal. haec igitur nisi praelibata generis specieique cognitione sciri non possunt.
passages.english: Unless you have first acquired knowledge and understanding of genera, species, properties and differences, you will never at any time discern the force of this. The same Aristotle states what primary substances are and what secondary ones are. He says that primary substances belong to individual and single bodies, as Cicero or Plato or Socrates is, while he called secondary substances the species, as man is, or the genera in which the species themselves are contained, as animal is. These things, therefore, cannot be known unless knowledge of genus and species has been acquired beforehand.

passages.original: idem sub- stantiae proprietates requirit, ut quasi inpresso aliquo signo, sic proprietate nota facilius quid substantia sit inuenire atque expedire possimus. atque hoc idem in accidentibus fecit. nam et quantitatis et qualitatis et ad aliquid relationis propria collegit, et idem magna apud Aristotelem cura diligentiaque conspicitur. uidesne ut sese quinque harum rerum uis in categorias interserat et praedicamentorum uirtutibus insepara- biliter colligetur? non mendax igitur Porphyrius de hac quinque harum rerum nobis in Categorias utilitate promisit.
passages.english: The same [Aristotle] looks for the properties of substance, so that, as if by some stamped mark, we may by means of a known property more easily find out and set forth what substance is. And he did the same in the case of accidents. For he collected the properties both of quantity and of quality and of the relation 'to something', and this same [knowledge] is seen in Aristotle with great care and diligence. Do you see how the force of these five things inserts itself into the Categories and is inseparably bound up with the powers of the predicaments? Porphyry, then, was not lying in what he promised us about the usefulness of these five things for the Categories.
passages.notes: 'idem ... conspicitur': the sense of 'idem' here is unclear; it may refer to the same treatment or be a resumptive 'likewise'.

passages.original: Definitionis uero disciplinam superius diximus praeter genera, species, differentias et propria non posse tractari. sed quoniam sunt quaedam genera quae genus habere non possunt, ut est substantia uel alia quae Aristoteles in praedicamentis constituit, dicat quis ad haec horum cognitionem nihil omnino prodesse. quod non sit in his a genere trahenda definitio in quibus genus inueniri non possit, quod, si qua res genus non haberet, species non esset; hoc ita posito ad generalissimorum generum definitionem nihil genera et species utilitatis habere.
passages.english: We said above that the discipline of definition cannot be dealt with apart from genera, species, differences and properties. But since there are certain genera which cannot have a genus, as substance is, or the others which Aristotle established in the Predicaments, someone might say that knowledge of these [five] is of no use whatever for them: that in things for which no genus can be found, a definition is not to be drawn from a genus, since, if a thing had no genus, it would not be a species; and that, this being granted, genera and species have no usefulness for the definition of the most general genera.

passages.original: ita ergo nunc de generibus, speciebus et ceteris quaerunt, utrum haec uere subsistentia et quodam- modo essentia constantiaque intellegantur, ut a corporalibus singulis uere atque integre ductam hominis speciem intel- legamus, an certe quadam animi imaginatione fingantur, ut ille Horatii uersus est : humano capiti ceruicem pictor equinam iunge re si uelit. quod neque est neque esse poterit, sed sola falsa mentis con- sideratione pingitur. nimis acute subtilis inquisitio atque ad rem maxime profutura! scienda enim sunt utrum uere sint, nec esse de his disputationem considerationemque, si non sint.
passages.english: So now they ask about genera, species and the rest in this way: whether these are understood as truly subsisting and, in a certain manner, as having essence and stability, so that we understand the species of man as truly and wholly drawn from single corporeal things, or whether they are certainly feigned by some imagination of the mind, as in that verse of Horace: "if a painter should wish to join a horse's neck to a human head." This neither is nor ever could be, but is painted solely by a false consideration of the mind. A very acute and subtle inquiry, and one that will be of the greatest use to the matter! For it must be known whether they truly exist, and that there is no disputation or consideration about them if they do not exist.

passages.original: sunt enim illa, ut ipse ait, grauioris tractatus; quam doctrinam a Peripate- ticis acceptam, id est ab Aristotelicis, se sequi confessus est. nam Stoici, qui de his quoque rebus tractare uoluerunt, non omnino a Porphyrio suscipiuntur, atque ideo ait se a Peripateticis rationem disputationis accipere. — Tunc me Fabius ita percunctatus : Quid est, inquit, quod dudum dixeras, cum a te de incorporalibus tractaretur, esse quasdam incor- poralitates quae circa corpus semper consisterent, ut sunt primae incorporalitates post terminos?
passages.english: For those things, as he himself says, belong to a weightier treatment; and he has acknowledged that he follows the teaching received from the Peripatetics, that is, from the Aristotelians. For the Stoics, who also wished to treat of these matters, are not at all taken up by Porphyry, and therefore he says that he takes his method of discussion from the Peripatetics. — Then Fabius questioned me thus: "What is it," he said, "that you said a while ago, when you were treating of incorporeal things, that there are certain incorporealities which always exist around a body, such as are the first incorporealities after the boundaries?"
passages.notes: Fabius is Boethius' interlocutor in the dialogue; not otherwise identified.

passages.original: quae genera causarum Graeci in rhetorica arte genera esse non putant, sed σχήματα uocant id est figuras, genera autem sola principalia accipiunt. demonstratiuum, deliberatiuum scilicet et iudiciale. quae ipsa ειδη ρητορικής uocant, id est species rhetoricae, genera uero causarum. tertium uero genus est id quod Porphyrius ponit, id est sub quo differentiis distributae species sup- ponuntur. sed quoniam de tertio genere tractaturus est, Victorini culpam uel, si ita contingit, emendationem aequi bonique faciamus.
passages.english: The Greeks in the art of rhetoric do not consider these kinds of cases to be genera, but call them schēmata, that is, figures, and accept as genera only the principal ones, namely the demonstrative, the deliberative and the judicial. These they call eidē rhētorikēs, that is, species of rhetoric, but genera of cases. The third genus is the one Porphyry posits, that is, that under which species, distributed by differences, are placed. But since he is going to treat of the third genus, let us take in good part Victorinus' fault or, if it so happens, his correction.

passages.original: Eorum quae dicuntur, alia ad unitatem dicuntur, sicut sunt omnia indiuidua, ut est Socrates et hic et illud, alia quae ad multitudinem, ut sunt genera <et> species et differentiae et propria et accidentia. haec enim communiter, non unius proprie appel- lationis sunt.
passages.english: Of the things that are said, some are said with reference to unity, as are all individuals, such as Socrates, and 'this' and 'that'; others with reference to multitude, as are genera, species, differences, properties and accidents. For these are common, and are not properly the designation of a single thing.
passages.notes: The angle brackets <et> mark an editorial supplement; it is translated. 'appel- lationis' is a line-break split for 'appellationis'.

passages.original: nam si dicas : quid est risibile? non absurdum est animal nominare. accidentia uero hoc modo principaliter in indiuiduis, secundo uero loco in speciebus sunt. nam si quis dicat ad singulos homines, ut puta Ciceronem, sedere uel stare uel quod aliud libet, in specie hominis eadem quoque conuenire necesse est. nam si Cicero sedet, sedet etiam homo, si Cicero ambulat, ambulat etiam homo. ergo si qua accidentia uenerint ab indiuiduis et ea tracta in speciebus consederint, ad ipsa quoque accidentia dici poterit genus. quid est enim ambulans, si quis interroget, merito animal dicitur. nihil enim ambulare nisi animal potest. porro autem sub speciebus indi- uidua sunt, ut Cicero et Virgilius sub homine, atque de indi- uiduo genus speciei praedicari potest. nam si interrogaueris, quid est Cicero, merito animal dicas. genus igitur et ad speciem et ad differentias et ad accidentia et ad propria et ad indiuidua nominatur.
passages.english: For if you say, "What is the risible?" it is not absurd to name animal. Accidents, however, are in this way principally in individuals, and secondarily in species. For if someone says of individual men, for instance Cicero, that he sits or stands or anything else you like, the same things must also belong to the species man. For if Cicero sits, man also sits; if Cicero walks, man also walks. Therefore, if any accidents have come from individuals and, drawn from them, have settled in species, the genus can also be said of those accidents themselves. For if anyone asks what the walking thing is, it is rightly said to be an animal, for nothing but an animal can walk. Further, under species are individuals, as Cicero and Virgil under man, and the genus of the species can be predicated of the individual. For if you ask what Cicero is, you would rightly say an animal. The genus, therefore, is predicated of the species, of the differences, of accidents, of properties and of individuals.

passages.original: ita ergo species de proprio praedicatur ut pari. sed quoniam sub speciebus singillatim indiuidua sunt — indiui- dua autem uocamus quae in nullas species neque in aliquas iam alias partes diuidi possunt, ut est Cato uel Plato uel Cicero et quicquid hominum singulorum est; hos enim in nullis partibus diuidis, ut animal in species, hominem scilicet atque equum, hominem ipsum specialem et singulos circumplecten- tem in Catonem, Platonem, Virgilium et omnes singillatim homines distributos;
passages.english: In this way, then, the species is predicated of the property as of an equal. But since under species there are individuals one by one — and we call individuals those things which can be divided neither into any species nor into any further parts, as Cato or Plato or Cicero and whatever single men there are; for you divide these into no parts, as [you divide] animal into species, namely man and horse, [and] man himself, as a species embracing the single ones, into Cato, Plato, Virgil and all men distributed one by one;
passages.notes: The sentence is incomplete; it continues beyond the passage.

passages.original: indiuidua uero quoniam sub se nihil ha|bent ubi secari distribuique possint, ad nihil aliud praedicantur nisi ad se ipsa, quae singula atque una sunt. atque hoc est quod ait: eorum quae dicuntur, alia ad unitatem dicuntur, sicut omnia indiuidua, ut est Socrates et hic et illud, alia quae ad multitudinem, ut sunt genera et species et differentiae et propria et accidentia. haec enim communiter, non unius proprie appel- lationis sunt. simile est ac si diceret : haec enim commu- niter ad plurima praedicantur, non ad unitatem sicut indiuidua.
passages.english: But individuals, since they have nothing beneath them into which they can be cut and distributed, are predicated with reference to nothing else except themselves, which are single and one. And this is what he says: 'Of the things that are said, some are said with reference to unity, as all individuals, such as Socrates, and "this" and "that"; others with reference to multitude, as are genera, species, differences, properties and accidents. For these are common, and are not properly the designation of a single thing.' It is as if he were saying: for these are predicated in common of very many things, not with reference to unity, as individuals are.

passages.original: distant autem, quod quamuis utraque ad plurima praedicentur et in eo quod quid sit, genus praedicatur ad res specie dif- ferentes, species uero dicitur ad res tantum numero differentes. quod Porphyrius sic demonstrat :
passages.english: They differ, however, in that, although both are predicated of many things and in respect of what [a thing] is, the genus is predicated of things differing in species, whereas the species is said of things differing only in number. Porphyry shows this as follows:

passages.original: itaque uel si prius rem dixeris, postea definitionem subieceris, uera erit, ut est ‘homo est animal rationale, mortale, risus et disciplinae perceptibile’, sin uero conuerteris et prius definitionem, postea rem dixeris, ut si dicas ‘animal quod fuerit rationale, mortale, risus et disci- plinae perceptibile homo est’, haec quoque uera est. ita semper, ut definitiones uerae sint, neque plus neque minus in defini- tionibus oportet aptari, sed aequali|ter definitiones conuenien- terque disponi. quod Porphyrius scilicet non ignorans ait se neque plus neque minus effecisse generis definitionem.
passages.english: So, whether you state the thing first and then add the definition, it will be true, as in 'man is a rational, mortal animal, capable of laughter and of learning', or if you reverse it and state the definition first and the thing afterwards, as if you say 'an animal which is rational, mortal, capable of laughter and of learning is man', this too is true. Thus always, for definitions to be true, neither more nor less must be fitted into the definitions, but definitions must be arranged equally and fittingly. Porphyry, of course, not unaware of this, says that he has made the definition of genus neither more nor less [than it should be].

passages.original: sed quia hoc in magis speciebus non euenit, ut ali- quando de specie differentibus praedicentur, haec definitio posterior solius magis speciei definitio est et eam ceterae sub- alternae species excludunt atque reiciunt. quod Porphyrius ita demonstrat : Sed haec definitio eius speciei est quae magis spe- cies dicitur, aliae uero definitiones erunt etiam illa- rum quae non sunt magis species.
passages.english: But since this does not happen in the most specific species, that they are at some time predicated of things differing in species, this latter definition is the definition of the most specific species alone, and the other, subaltern species exclude and reject it. Porphyry shows this as follows: "But this definition belongs to that species which is called most specific, while the other definitions will also belong to those which are not most specific species."
passages.notes: "magis species" is Boethius' term for the most specific (lowest) species (species specialissima).

passages.original: quod si ita est, non est dubium genus quoque generis illius quod ad illud ad quod species praedicabatur, poterat praedicari, etiam id quoque de eo <ad> quod species et genus speciei praedicabatur, praedicari posse. nam si quis dicat Ciceronem esse hominem, cum animal hominis genus sit, non erit absurdum Ciceronem animal praedicari, et cum animalis ipsius substantia genus sit, non erit inconueniens Ciceronem substantiam praedicari, quoniam quae supersunt, de subterioribus praedicantur et ea quae sub|teriora sunt, si qua alia sibi subteriora habeant, illud primum genus habebunt etiam ista subteriora et de his non inconuenienter praedicabi- tur.
passages.english: If this is so, there is no doubt that the genus also of that genus which could be predicated of that of which the species was predicated can likewise itself be predicated of that of which the species and the genus of the species were predicated. For if someone says that Cicero is a man, since animal is the genus of man, it will not be absurd for Cicero to be predicated [as] animal; and since substance is the genus of animal itself, it will not be unfitting for Cicero to be predicated [as] substance, since the things that are higher are predicated of the lower, and the things that are lower, if they have any other things lower than themselves, these lower things too will have that first genus, and it will not unfittingly be predicated of them.
passages.notes: The first sentence is convoluted and the syntax awkward (the edition supplies <ad>); translated according to its evident sense.

passages.original: eodem enim modo ex materia et figura species cuiuscumque illius fictionis formata est, quemadmodum ex genere uel differentiis species cuiuscumque illius animantis inanimantisue formatur. quod Victorinus scilicet intellexisse minus uidetur. nam quod Porphyrius άνάλογον dixit, id est proportionale, ille sic accepit quasi άλογον diceret, id est inrationale. atque ideo in loco ubi habet hoc modo scriptum :
passages.english: For the form of any such sculpted figure is formed out of matter and shape in the same way as the species of any animate or inanimate thing is formed out of genus and differences. This, it seems, Victorinus understood too little. For what Porphyry called analogon, that is, proportional, he took as though [Porphyry] had said alogon, that is, irrational. And so in the passage where he has written it thus:
passages.notes: The passage breaks off before the quotation of Victorinus' rendering.

passages.original: accidens uero ante praedicatur de indiuiduis et postea de speciebus. nam si quis dicat : homo sedet, quod est accidens separabile, cum quicum- que singulum hominem, id est indiuiduum, sedere uiderit, tunc id et de specie praedicat, ut dicat : quoniam Cicero sedet, Cicero autem homo est, homo sedet. eodem modo inseparabile de speciebus et de indiuiduis praedicatur.
passages.english: Accident, however, is predicated first of individuals and afterwards of species. For if someone says "man sits", which is a separable accident, when he has seen some single man, that is, an individual, sitting, then he predicates it also of the species, so as to say: since Cicero sits, and Cicero is a man, a man sits. In the same way the inseparable [accident] is predicated of species and of individuals.

passages.original: differentia enim quadrupes in bouis et in equi et in canis specie est et differentia rationalis hominis et del. species uero numquam aliis nisi solis sub se indiuiduis praeest. num- quam enim alia res homo est nisi quod est indiuiduum, ut est Socrates et Plato et Cicero, unde fit ut sublata differentia species quoque tollatur, nam si sustuleris rationale, hominem sustuleris, si uero sustuleris speciem, differentia manet, nam si sustuleris hominem, rationalis del differentia remanebit.
passages.english: For the difference 'four-footed' is found in the species of ox, of horse and of dog, and the difference 'rational' [in the species] of man and of god. A species, however, is never set over anything except only the individuals beneath it. For 'man' is never anything else except what is an individual, such as Socrates, Plato and Cicero. Hence it happens that when the difference is removed the species is also removed, for if you remove 'rational', you will have removed man; but if you remove the species, the difference remains, for if you remove man, the difference 'rational' of god will remain.
passages.notes: 'del' (twice) is evidently a scanning error for 'dei' (of god).
